questions.q: What is the primary way the government collects money to provide public services?
questions.a: The primary way is through taxes. A wrong answer here suggests the student hasn't grasped the basic link between government services and public funding.

questions.q: Why is an income tax called a "direct" tax?
questions.a: It is called "direct" because the person earning the money pays the tax directly to the government themselves. A wrong answer indicates confusion between paying a tax directly versus paying it hidden inside the price of a product.

questions.q: If you buy a notebook and pay tax as part of the price, is this a direct or indirect tax? Explain why.
questions.a: This is an indirect tax because you aren't sending the money to the government yourself; the shopkeeper includes it in the price and sends it later. A wrong answer shows the student is not yet able to apply the "direct vs. indirect" distinction to real-life shopping scenarios.

questions.q: Compare a corporate tax (on company profits) with the tax paid on a packet of biscuits. Which one is direct and which is indirect?
questions.a: Corporate tax is direct (the company pays it on its own profits) and the biscuit tax is indirect (the consumer pays it as part of the price). A wrong answer reveals a failure to analyze the source and method of payment for these different entities.

questions.q: Should a government rely only on taxes, or are there other ways to earn money? Is it fair for the government to take money from citizens?
questions.a: Governments use taxes because it is the most reliable way to fund public needs, though they also earn from fines and service charges. It is considered fair because these services (like fire safety or roads) benefit everyone in the community. A wrong answer shows a lack of understanding of the "participatory" nature of democracy.

questions.q: Imagine your town wants to build a new park. How would you explain to a classmate why the town needs to collect money from local businesses and residents to build it?
questions.a: A good answer explains that the park is a "public good" that everyone uses, so everyone must contribute a small amount so the government has the budget to build and maintain it. A poor answer fails to connect the cost of infrastructure to the need for public funding.
